name: Waymo's AI and Safety Research: Autonomous Driving at Scale
title: Waymo's AI and Safety Research: Autonomous Driving at Scale
answer: Waymo's website publishes detailed technical and safety research on its autonomous driving AI, including the Waymo Foundation Model, the Waymo World Model for simulation, scaling laws for motion planning, and its safety framework. The most useful single item is the December 2025 report describing the Foundation Model's Think Fast and Think Slow architecture, which combines a Sensor Fusion Encoder with a Driving VLM trained using Gemini to handle rare and complex scenarios.

sections.body: Waymo, the Alphabet-owned autonomous driving company, publishes a blog and research hub at waymo.com. The pages reviewed span May 2018 to March 2026 and include technical reports on the Waymo Foundation Model, the Waymo World Model, scaling laws in autonomous driving, and the company's safety framework, alongside news and public education posts. Waymo began in 2009 as the Google Self-Driving Car Project and operates a fully autonomous ride-hailing service called Waymo One.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Waymo describes a unified AI ecosystem built on the Waymo Foundation Model, comprising the Driver, Simulator, and Critic. The model uses a Think Fast and Think Slow architecture with two components: a Sensor Fusion Encoder that fuses camera, lidar, and radar inputs over time to produce objects, semantics, and rich embeddings, and a Driving VLM trained using Gemini that leverages world knowledge to understand rare, novel, and complex semantic scenarios. Both feed into a World Decoder that predicts other road users' behavior, produces high-definition maps, generates trajectories, and signals for validation. Waymo adapts the Foundation Model to Driver, Simulator, and Critic tasks to create large Teacher models, then distills them into smaller Student models for real-time decision making and large-scale simulation. The Waymo World Model, built on Google DeepMind's Genie 3, generates photorealistic and interactive 3D environments with camera and lidar outputs, and allows engineers to modify simulations through driving action control, scene layout control, and language prompts. Waymo's scaling study used an internal dataset of 500,000 hours of driving and found that motion forecasting quality follows a power-law as a function of training compute, similar to large language models.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Waymo reports well over 100 million fully autonomous miles in December 2025 and nearly 200 million by February 2026, with more than 300 million autonomous kilometers cited in March 2026. It claims a more than ten-fold reduction in crashes with serious injuries compared to human drivers, and a 93% improvement in safety performance. The scaling study used 500,000 hours of driving data and compared models of roughly 1 million and 30 million parameters. Waymo serves over half a million trips every week across 10 U.S. cities. In 2018 it reported reducing pedestrian detection error rate by 100x with Google Brain and training neural networks up to 15x more efficiently with TPUs.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: This source gives a reader following AI in transportation a rare operator-level view of how foundation models, vision-language models, and generative world models are being applied to a safety-critical driving task. The scaling laws study offers evidence that motion planning and forecasting improve predictably with data and compute, which is directly relevant to anyone assessing the trajectory of autonomous vehicle capability. The safety framework and crash-rate comparisons provide a public methodology for evaluating AV safety claims, and the World Model work shows how simulation is being used to test rare and counterfactual scenarios that cannot be safely or frequently encountered on real roads.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Transportation

sections.body: The material is published by Waymo about its own technology and operations, so safety and performance claims are self-reported and not independently verified within these pages. Several posts are promotional or educational rather than technical, and the safety framework dates from 2020 while the scaling study and World Model posts are more recent. The pages do not provide raw datasets, full peer-reviewed papers, or detailed regulatory filings, and coverage of markets outside the United States is limited to a Tokyo partnership announcement.
